note: Two things that belong together: who else can help with this recipe, and what this recipe asks of whoever is cooking it. Both are read off the recipe's own steps rather than authored per dish, so they work on all 242 recipes instead of the eight somebody had time to annotate.

wording.note: A note on the words used here, because they were chosen carefully. Recipes are not sorted by how good a cook you are — they are sorted by what they ask for. A dish that asks for four things at once is not better than one that asks for one thing; it is just a different evening. Nothing in this app is labeled easy, basic, beginner or simple as a judgment of the person reading it, and nothing is labeled advanced as a compliment.
wording.kidsNote: The same goes for children. A five-year-old tearing basil is cooking — not helping, not playing at it. The jobs below are real jobs with real reasons, which is why every one of them says what it teaches.

ages.label: 2 to 3
ages.blurb: Standing on a chair, in the way, delighted. Everything at this age is about touching food and being somewhere useful.
ages.supervision: Beside an adult the whole time, and nothing near heat.

ages.label: 4 to 5
ages.blurb: Old enough to follow one instruction at a time and proud of finishing something. This is the age where measuring and mixing genuinely help.
ages.supervision: Adult in the kitchen, heat and blades still off limits.

ages.label: 6 to 8
ages.blurb: Can read a step, use a table knife on soft things, and be trusted with a task while you do something else in the same room.
ages.supervision: Adult nearby. First lessons with a peeler and scissors happen here.

ages.label: 9 to 12
ages.blurb: Ready for real knives and real heat, taught properly rather than avoided. Most children this age can cook a whole dish with somebody in the room.
ages.supervision: Taught once, then watched, then trusted.

ages.label: 13 and up
ages.blurb: Capable of the whole recipe, start to finish, including the deciding. The useful thing an adult can do here is get out of the way and eat what is made.
ages.supervision: None required. Being asked to cook one dinner a week is how this becomes a life skill instead of a chore.

jobs.name: Wash the vegetables
jobs.teaches: That food comes out of the ground, and that grit at the bottom of a bowl of greens is why we do this.
jobs.safe: Cold water and a colander. Nothing sharp involved.

jobs.name: Tear the herbs and greens
jobs.teaches: That soft herbs bruise when they are cut and torn edges hold more aroma — the first real cooking fact most children learn, and one plenty of adults do not know.

jobs.name: Stir it
jobs.teaches: Patience, mostly. Also that a batter stirred to death goes tough, which is the reason muffins say 'until just combined'.
jobs.safe: In a bowl off the heat, or at the stove with an adult holding the pan handle.

jobs.name: Measure and pour
jobs.teaches: Fractions, honestly, before anybody calls them fractions. Also that baking measurements are rules and savory ones are suggestions.
jobs.safe: Do it over a bowl, not over the pan.

jobs.name: Mash it
jobs.teaches: How much texture is a choice — half-mashed beans and fully mashed beans are two different dishes.
jobs.safe: A fork or a masher, in a bowl, once the food has cooled enough to touch.

jobs.name: Scatter the topping
jobs.teaches: That the last thing on is the first thing tasted, which is the whole reason this step exists.
jobs.safe: Off the heat, at the table.

jobs.name: Spread and layer
jobs.teaches: Building a thing in order, and that the crisp part goes on top of the wet part or it stops being crisp.
jobs.safe: A butter knife or the back of a spoon.

jobs.name: Crack the eggs
jobs.teaches: A firm tap on a flat surface, not the rim of the bowl. Crack into a separate cup first and a stray shell costs nothing.
jobs.safe: Wash hands afterward, before touching anything else.

jobs.name: Peel it
jobs.teaches: That a peeler goes away from you and the vegetable lies flat on a board rather than being held in the air.
jobs.safe: A Y-peeler is safer and easier than a straight one. Peel onto a board, not into a hand.

jobs.name: Cut the soft things
jobs.teaches: Knife work, starting with a tool nobody is frightened of. Kitchen scissors on herbs, scallions and greens; a table knife on a banana or a cooked potato.
jobs.safe: Scissors and table knives only at this age. The claw grip and a real knife come next.

jobs.name: Grate the cheese
jobs.teaches: That cheese grated at the table tastes stronger than the same cheese stirred in — you smell it on the way to your mouth.
jobs.safe: Stop while there is still a piece to hold. A grater guard, or hand the last inch to an adult.

jobs.name: Squeeze the lemon
jobs.teaches: The single most useful thing in this whole app: taste it before the lemon, taste it after, and understand what acid does. Do this once with a child and they have learned something most adults never articulate.
jobs.safe: Watch for cuts on hands — lemon juice finds every one.

jobs.name: Be the taster
jobs.teaches: Everything. A child who is asked whether it needs more salt, and whose answer is actually used, is being taught to cook. This is the most valuable job on the list and it costs nothing.
jobs.safe: A clean spoon each time, and let it cool first.

jobs.name: Run the timer
jobs.teaches: That cooking runs on time as much as on ingredients, and that most things are checked before the timer rather than at it.
jobs.safe: Nothing to it. A real job with real consequences, which is why children take it seriously.

jobs.name: Set the table
jobs.teaches: That dinner is a thing the household makes together rather than a thing that appears. Also water on the table, which is the one hydration habit on this app's list that actually needs a person to do it.

jobs.name: Work the stove
jobs.teaches: Heat management, which is the skill that separates somebody who follows recipes from somebody who cooks. Start with the handle turned in and a dry towel already in the other hand.
jobs.safe: Taught deliberately: pan handles turned inward, add food away from you, never a wet hand on a hot handle. Avoiding the stove until eighteen does not make anybody safer.

jobs.name: In and out of the oven
jobs.teaches: Where the hot parts of an oven are, and that a sheet pan wants both hands and a clear landing spot decided before the door opens.
jobs.safe: Dry mitts — a wet one conducts heat straight through. Say out loud where the pan is going before it comes out.

jobs.name: Plate it up
jobs.teaches: That how food looks changes how it tastes, and that a pile in the middle of a warm plate beats a thin layer across a cold one.
jobs.safe: Warm plates rather than hot ones for this.

hazards.note: Words that mean a step belongs to an adult, or to an older child being taught rather than left to it. Matched per step, so one dangerous step does not put a whole recipe out of reach of a five-year-old who could happily do the other six.
hazards.say: This step has heat, a blade or something heavy in it. It belongs to a grown-up, or to an older child who has been shown how — once, properly, rather than never.

kidsNote: Children who cook eat more of what they cooked. That is the whole argument, and it works better than any conversation about vegetables ever has.

ladder.name: Short and forgiving
ladder.blurb: Few steps, nothing to time precisely, and hard to get wrong. Good for a Tuesday, good for a first attempt, good when the kitchen is full of people.

ladder.name: One thing to get right
ladder.blurb: Straightforward except for a single moment that decides how it comes out — the browning, the timing, the not-stirring. That moment is the whole lesson.
ladder.asks: Paying attention once, at the right time.

ladder.name: A few things at once
ladder.blurb: Two or three pans, or a sauce going while something roasts. Nothing here is difficult on its own; the skill being asked for is keeping track.
ladder.asks: Prep done before the heat goes on.

ladder.name: Worth an afternoon
ladder.blurb: Long, or fiddly, or both, and the reason to cook it is the cooking. Not better than anything above it — just a different kind of day.
ladder.asks: Time, and the willingness to spend it.

teaches.note: One thing each recipe quietly teaches, matched from what its own method actually does. A cook who reads eighty of these has picked up eighty techniques without ever opening a technique book, which is the only way most people ever learn them.

lessons.title: Deglazing
lessons.body: The brown crust stuck to the pan is not mess, it is concentrated flavor that came out of the food. A splash of liquid dissolves it back into the dish. Everything that makes a pan sauce taste like something is on the bottom of the pan before the liquid goes in.

lessons.title: Blooming spices
lessons.body: Most spice aromatics dissolve in fat and not in water. Thirty to sixty seconds in hot oil before the liquid goes in is the difference between tasting a spice and tasting the idea of one — and past ninety seconds they burn, which is why the window is stated so exactly.

lessons.title: Leaving it alone
lessons.body: Browning needs a surface to stay against the pan long enough to get above 300°F. Every stir starts that clock over. Doing nothing for four minutes is an active cooking skill and it is the one most people skip.

lessons.title: Emulsifying
lessons.body: Starchy pasta water is what turns oil and cheese into a sauce that clings instead of a puddle that slides off. The starch holds the fat and water together. This is the whole secret of Italian pasta, and it costs one ladle of water you were about to pour down the sink.

lessons.title: Resting
lessons.body: Food keeps cooking after it comes off the heat, and the fibers are holding their liquid under pressure. Five minutes lets the temperature even out and the juice stay in the food instead of running onto the board.

lessons.title: Salting the water
lessons.body: It is the only chance to season pasta or a vegetable from the inside. It should taste noticeably salty — most of it goes down the drain, and what stays behind is the difference between pasta that tastes of something and pasta that needs rescuing with sauce.

lessons.title: Finishing with acid
lessons.body: Acid is volatile and goes dull with heat, so the last squeeze goes in off the burner. This is the single most common thing missing from home cooking and the fastest fix for a dish nobody can find the fault in.

lessons.title: Not crowding the pan
lessons.body: Food releases water. If there is nowhere for it to go, it collects and the food steams instead of browning. Empty space in a pan is an ingredient, and two batches genuinely beat one.

lessons.title: Everything ready first
lessons.body: Not a French affectation. In anything that cooks in under ten minutes there is no time to chop, so the chopping decides whether the cooking works. This is why stir-fries fail.

lessons.title: Tempering dairy
lessons.body: Yogurt, sour cream and milk split when they hit a boil — the proteins clump and squeeze out water. Warm them with a ladle of the hot liquid first, or stir them in off the heat, and they stay smooth.

lessons.title: Drying the surface
lessons.body: Every drop of surface water has to boil off before anything can brown, and nothing browns below about 300°F. Ten seconds with a towel is the cheapest upgrade in cooking.

lessons.title: Salting in layers
lessons.body: Salt added early does work — it pulls water out of onions so they brown, and it seasons from the inside. Salt added at the end only sits on top. The same total amount tastes like more when it goes in over time.
